274.title: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (1 of 7)
274.hook: so, what do you do? the third path asks a harder question
274.tomorrow: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (2 of 7)
274.howItsDone: In Vedanta, jnana yoga is practiced by studying the Upanishads with a teacher, reflecting on them, and meditating on the self as the witness of body and mind; 'not this, not this' (neti neti) is one of its classic tools.

segments.voice: Last week: bhakti yoga, and the line love as the road. Nine doors, the Tamil saints, Mira, Tulsidas, Surdas, and a street full of kirtan. Today, the third path.

You're at a party, and someone you've just met asks the question. So, what do you do? You answer: a job title, maybe where you live, whether you have kids, what you studied. Now imagine they don't accept any of it. No, not your job. Who are you? You try your name. That's a label your parents picked. Your personality? That's changed a lot since you were eight. Your body? Most of it has been rebuilt since you were a child. Keep going, and it gets strange fast. The third path of yoga starts right there, at the question you can't quite answer.
screen: `SO, WHAT DO YOU DO?` → `NO: WHO ARE YOU?` → `THE QUESTION YOU CAN'T ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Jnana comes from the Sanskrit root jna, to know. It's a cousin of the English word know, and the Greek gnosis. But jnana doesn't mean information. You can't look it up. It means knowing the way you know you're awake: direct, from the inside. Karma yoga asked what you do. Bhakti asked who you love. Jnana asks who is doing and loving in the first place. One of the oldest teachers of this road is a sage in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad named Yajnavalkya, and he gives it a two-word tool. Neti, neti. Not this, not this. Asked to describe the self, the real I, he refused to give it a label. Whatever you can point at is not it. Not the body. Not the breath. Not the thoughts, not the feelings. It sounds like a riddle, but the logic is simple. Anything you can observe is something you're observing, so it can't be the observer. Elsewhere in the same Upanishad, Yajnavalkya asks: by what would one know the knower? Your eye can see everything except itself. So the jnana path isn't adding knowledge. It's subtraction: peeling off everything that turns out to be an object, until what's left is the one who was looking all along. This week: practicing that peeling, the method of the great teacher Shankara, and a strange, fierce little book called the Ashtavakra Gita. The line for the week is short: who am I?
screen: `JNA — TO KNOW, FROM THE INSIDE.` · `NETI, NETI: NOT THIS, NOT THIS.` · `WHO KNOWS THE KNOWER?` · `SUBTRACTION, NOT ADDITION.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Notice the weight of your body on the seat and say inwardly, not this; then the breath, not this; then a thought passing through, not this, either. Don't push anything away; just notice it's being noticed, and rest as the one noticing, without trying to describe it. If it slips away, begin again.
Jnana yoga. The path of knowledge: not information, but knowing from the inside who you are. Its first tool is neti, neti, not this, not this.
Your line: who am I? Every answer you can point at is not quite it. Day two seventy-four.

275.title: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (2 of 7)
275.hook: ten travelers cross a river, count themselves, and find only nine
275.tomorrow: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (3 of 7)
275.howItsDone: Advaita Vedanta teachers often use the parable of the tenth man to show that self-knowledge isn't gaining something new but recognizing what was always present; students then practice discerning the witness from what it witnesses.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jnana yoga, and Yajnavalkya's two words, neti, neti. Not this, not this. Today, a story Vedanta teachers tell.

Ten friends set out on a trip together, and they have to ford a fast river. They wade across, holding on to each other, and scramble up the far bank, soaked. The leader, to be safe, counts heads. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine. Nine. He counts again. Nine. Someone's been swept away. Each of the others counts, and each gets nine too. They sit down on the riverbank and weep for their lost friend.
screen: `TEN FRIENDS CROSS A RIVER.` → `ONE, TWO… NINE.` → `THEY WEEP FOR THE LOST ONE.`

segments.voice: A traveler walking by asks what's wrong. They tell him: there were ten of us, and one has drowned. He looks at them, and counts. Ten. He asks the leader to count again. Nine. Then the traveler touches the leader on the shoulder and says: you are the tenth. That's the whole story. It's told in Advaita Vedanta texts because it shows how neti neti works in practice. The leader wasn't missing. He was doing the counting, so he never counted himself. He was looking everywhere but at the looker. And notice: nothing new was found. No one came out of the river. The grief ended the moment he recognized what had been there the whole time. That's why jnana is called knowledge, not achievement. You don't become the self. You stop leaving it out of the count. So how do you practice it? Neti neti in real life is a kind of honest sorting. When you feel, I am angry, look closer: anger is showing up, and something is aware of it. Not this. When you think, I am a failure, look closer: a thought is showing up. Not this. You don't deny the anger or the thought. You just stop counting them as the counter. What's left is the one who was looking. The Upanishads have a phrase for this recognition, and later teachers repeat it again and again: you are that.
screen: `THE TRAVELER COUNTS: TEN.` · `YOU ARE THE TENTH.` · `NOTHING NEW WAS FOUND.` · `STOP LEAVING YOURSELF OUT.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Count, like the leader on the riverbank: one, the body sitting; two, the breath; three, a sound in the room; four, a thought; five, whatever mood is here. Then pause and ask: who's counting? Don't answer with a word; just turn toward the counter, the way the traveler turned the leader around, and when counting starts again, let it.
Jnana yoga, in practice. Neti neti sets aside what can be counted, the body, the thoughts, the moods, and turns you toward the counter. You are the tenth.
Your line: who am I? The one counting was never missing. Day two seventy-five, counted.

276.title: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (3 of 7)
276.hook: a husband offers to split the property; his wife asks for something else
276.tomorrow: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (4 of 7)
276.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, students traditionally study the Upanishads and Shankara's commentaries with a teacher (shravana), work through doubts and questions (manana), and then practice sustained contemplation (nididhyasana).

segments.voice: Yesterday: ten friends, a river, and the leader who forgot to count himself. You are the tenth. Today, a question worth more than a fortune.

The sage Yajnavalkya, the one who said neti neti, decides to leave home and live as a wandering monk. He has two wives, and he calls one of them, Maitreyi, to settle things. Let me divide what I have between you and Katyayani, he says. It's a fair, sensible offer. Maitreyi asks one question. If this whole earth, full of wealth, were mine, would it make me immortal? No, he says. Your life would be like the life of the rich. That's all. And she says: then what would I do with something that won't make me immortal? Tell me what you know instead.
screen: `LET ME DIVIDE WHAT I HAVE.` → `WOULD IT MAKE ME IMMORTAL?` → `TELL ME WHAT YOU KNOW INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya is delighted, and he teaches her. In that conversation in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, he gives a line that became the backbone of the jnana path. Paraphrased: the self is what should be seen. It should be heard about, reflected on, and deeply meditated on. Much later, the teacher Shankara and those who followed him made those verbs a method, three steps still taught in Vedanta schools. First, shravana: hearing. You listen to the teaching, from the Upanishads and from a teacher, carefully, the way Maitreyi listened. Not skimming. Hearing. Second, manana: reflecting. You argue with what you've heard and raise every doubt. Does this make sense? What about this objection? Shankara didn't want blind belief; he spent pages answering objections. Third, nididhyasana: deep, sustained meditation. Once the doubts have settled, you dwell on the teaching until it's no longer an idea you hold but the way you see. Hear it, test it, soak in it. It's how you learn anything that really changes you: a friend says you're kinder than you think, you argue with it, and slowly, over months, you live into it. Shankara also insisted on a teacher. Not a guru to worship blindly, but someone who has walked the road and can point, like the traveler who turned the leader around. And notice where this began. Not with a debate. With a woman who turned down her share of a fortune and asked for the truth.
screen: `MAITREYI TURNS DOWN THE FORTUNE.` · `SHRAVANA: HEARING.` · `MANANA: REFLECTING.` · `NIDIDHYASANA: SOAKING IN IT.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Take one small line, I am aware, and first just hear it, letting the words land. Then reflect: is it true right now, is there awareness here? Raise any doubt you honestly have. If it holds, soak in it: don't repeat the words, just rest in what they point to, the plain fact of being aware.
Jnana yoga, Shankara's method: shravana, manana, nididhyasana. Hearing the teaching, reflecting on it, and meditating on it until it becomes how you see.
Your line: who am I? On this road, even your doubts get a step of their own. See you next time.

277.title: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (4 of 7)
277.hook: on a narrow lane in Kashi, the great teacher tells a man to step aside, and the man asks who should move
277.tomorrow: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (5 of 7)
277.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers traditionally describe four qualifications for students of self-knowledge (sadhana chatushtaya): discrimination, dispassion, the six virtues of a steady mind, and longing for freedom; students work on these alongside study.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maitreyi, who turned down a fortune, and Shankara's three steps. Hearing, reflecting, soaking in it. Today, what a student needs to walk this road.

There's a story told about Shankara in Varanasi, the holy city also called Kashi. He's walking to the river with his students, and on a narrow lane a man comes toward them with his dogs, a man from a community that the purity rules of the day kept at a distance. Shankara says what the custom said to say: move aside. The man doesn't move. He asks: which should move away from which? This body from that body? Both are made of food. Or this self from that self? There's only one. Shankara, the story says, stopped, and bowed to him.
screen: `A NARROW LANE IN KASHI.` → `MOVE ASIDE.` → `WHICH SHOULD MOVE FROM WHICH?`

segments.voice: Tradition says Shankara then composed five verses, the Manisha Panchakam, each ending: whoever sees this way is my teacher, whatever his birth. It's a humbling story to find at the center of a great teacher's life, and that's partly why people tell it. Knowing the teaching isn't the same as living it. So what does living it take? Texts in Shankara's tradition, like the Vivekachudamani, list four qualifications a student needs. Not degrees. Qualities. First, viveka: discrimination, in the old sense. Telling the lasting from the passing. The body, the mood, the reputation: passing. What's aware of them: lasting. Second, vairagya: dispassion. Not hating the world, just loosening your grip on what passes. You still enjoy the meal; you just don't need it to save you. Third, six treasures of a steady mind. Calm. Self-restraint. Doing your own duty without fuss. Patience with heat and cold, praise and blame. Trust in the teacher and the teaching. And focus. Fourth, “mumukshutva”: longing for freedom. The Vivekachudamani says that where dispassion and this longing are weak, calm and the rest are like water seen in a desert. Maitreyi turning down the fortune? That was “mumukshutva”. And Shankara bowing on the lane? That was viveka catching up with him: the rule was about bodies, and the one he'd been teaching about was not a body at all. The man with the dogs had it the whole time.
screen: `VIVEKA: LASTING FROM PASSING.` · `VAIRAGYA: LOOSENING THE GRIP.` · `SIX TREASURES OF A STEADY MIND.` · `THE LONGING TO BE FREE.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Sort things gently as they arise: a sound, passing; a twinge in the knee, passing; a worry about tomorrow, a pleasant memory, passing too. Don't push any of it away; then notice what hasn't passed through all of it, the noticing, and rest there for a few breaths. If you want, remember the man on the lane, and let there be no one to step aside from.
Jnana yoga, and its four qualifications: viveka, telling lasting from passing; vairagya, dispassion; six treasures of a steady mind; and “mumukshutva”, the longing to be free.
Your line: who am I? On a lane in Kashi, it came back as a question: which should move from which? Two seventy-seven, done.

278.title: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (5 of 7)
278.hook: a boy bent in eight places walks into a king's court, and the court laughs
278.tomorrow: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (6 of 7)
278.howItsDone: The Ashtavakra Gita is read and chanted in many Advaita circles as a direct statement of non-dual teaching, often studied alongside the Upanishads; its opening questions from King Janaka frame the whole text.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the lane in Kashi, and the four qualifications. Discernment, dispassion, a steady mind, longing to be free. Your line: who am I?

An unborn child corrects his own father. The Mahabharata tells of a scholar named Kahoda who recited the Vedas while his wife was pregnant, and from inside the womb the child pointed out his mistakes. The father, stung, cursed him: you'll be born bent in eight places. Then Kahoda went to the court of King Janaka, lost a debate to the court's champion, and never came home. The boy was born bent, just as the curse said. They called him Ashtavakra: eight bends. At twelve he learned what had happened, and set out, crooked and limping, for that court to win his father back.
screen: `CORRECTED FROM THE WOMB.` → `ASHTAVAKRA: EIGHT BENDS.` → `A BOY GOES TO THE KING'S COURT.`

segments.voice: In the Mahabharata's telling, the boy talks his way past the gatekeeper, defeats the court's champion debater, and his father is restored. People love to tell a popular addition: when Ashtavakra walked in, the courtiers laughed at his body, and he laughed back. Why are you laughing? they asked. I thought this was an assembly of the wise, he said. It's a gathering of leather-workers. You only judge the skin. Whether that exchange is old or newer, it fits the book that carries his name. The Ashtavakra Gita is a short Sanskrit dialogue between the sage and King Janaka. Nobody knows when it was written, or by whom. Some readers on the jnana path prize it because it's so blunt. It opens with the king asking three questions. Paraphrased: how is knowledge gained? How will freedom come? How is detachment reached? Tell me this, my lord. Not how do I become a better person. Not how do I get to heaven. How do I know. How am I free. How do I let go. That's the whole jnana path in one breath. And notice who's asking: a king, with everything. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names Janaka as one who reached perfection through action, a king who lived in the world and wasn't owned by it. The answer he gets, tomorrow, doesn't ask him to give up his throne.
screen: `THE COURT LAUGHS AT THE BODY.` · `YOU ONLY JUDGE THE SKIN.` · `A KING ASKS THREE QUESTIONS.` · `KNOWLEDGE, FREEDOM, LETTING GO.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Ask Janaka's three questions for yourself, slowly, one per stretch of breathing: what do I actually know, for certain, right now? Where do I feel not free, just noticing, not fixing? What am I gripping, a plan, a person, an idea of myself? Let each question open without rushing an answer; the asking is the practice.
Jnana yoga, through the Ashtavakra Gita: a dialogue between a sage bent in eight places and King Janaka, who asks how to know, how to be free, how to let go.
Your line: who am I? The courtiers laughed, and saw only the skin. See you tomorrow.

279.title: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (6 of 7)
279.hook: a king asks for a long path; the sage says: right now
279.tomorrow: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (7 of 7)
279.howItsDone: Students of the Ashtavakra Gita often chant or read its first chapter slowly, pausing on each verse, and use its list of the five elements as a contemplation: noticing each as known, and resting as the knower.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ashtavakra, the sage of eight bends, and King Janaka's three questions. How do I know? How am I free? How do I let go? Your line: who am I? Today, the answer.

Anything worth having takes a long time, right? Learning an instrument: years. Getting in shape: months of mornings. So when a king asks how to be free, you'd expect a long program. Twelve years in a forest. A thousand rules. A ladder with a hundred rungs. Ashtavakra's answer starts gently, with a little advice about how to live. Then, a few verses in, it says something so bold you may read the line twice.
screen: `WORTH HAVING TAKES A LONG TIME.` → `A KING ASKS HOW TO BE FREE.` → `THEN THE ANSWER GETS BOLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening of the reply, paraphrased. If you want freedom, my child, treat the pull of the senses like poison, and drink forgiveness, honesty, kindness, contentment and truth like nectar. That's the gentle part: a good life, sensibly described. The next verse turns everything. You are not earth. You are not water, or fire, or air, or space. To be free, know yourself as the witness of all these: awareness itself. Neti neti again, in the king's own language. The old Indian list of five elements that make up everything, and the sage says: you're none of them. You're the one they appear to. Then the verse that stops people. If you set the body aside and rest in awareness, then right now, this very moment, you'll be happy, at peace, and free. Not after twelve years. Not after you've fixed your temper or your diet. Now. A little later he adds: right and wrong, pleasure and pain, belong to the mind, not to you. You're not the doer, not the one who enjoys the results. You were always free. Is that too easy? Teachers in the tradition say it isn't easy at all; it's simple, which is different. Nothing has to be built. But everything you keep counting as yourself has to be seen through, the way the leader by the river had to stop counting and turn around. That's why the Ashtavakra Gita is so loved on the jnana path. It doesn't give you a ladder. It points at the floor you're already standing on.
screen: `SENSES AS POISON, VIRTUES AS NECTAR.` · `YOU ARE NOT EARTH, WATER, FIRE.` · `THE WITNESS OF ALL THESE.` · `RIGHT NOW: HAPPY, AT PEACE, FREE.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Walk Ashtavakra's list slowly: earth, the weight of the body on the seat; water, the moisture in the mouth; fire, the warmth of the skin; air, the breath; space, the room around you, each one noticed, none of them what you are. Then, for a few breaths, rest as the one noticing, right now. If the mind says it's not working, that's a thought too: noticed.
Jnana yoga, in the Ashtavakra Gita's answer: you are not the elements, but the witness of them, awareness itself; rest there, and you're free now.
Your line: who am I? Not earth, not water, not fire: the one they appear to. That's day two seventy-nine.

280.title: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (7 of 7)
280.hook: think you're bound, and you are; think you're free, and you are
280.tomorrow: Advaita (Shankara): not-two; rope and snake in full; the Vivekachudamani opening (1 of 7)
280.howItsDone: Many Hindu teachers present karma, bhakti and jnana (often with raja yoga, meditation) as paths suited to different temperaments, while also teaching that they support one another; the Bhagavad Gita is the classic text that holds all three.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ashtavakra's bold answer. You are not the elements, but their witness; rest there, and you're free now. Your line: who am I? Today, the last day of jnana, and of the three paths.

Two people lose their jobs in the same week. One says: that's it, I'm finished. The other says: all right, what now? One spends the month replaying the meeting. The other starts making calls. Same company, same letter, same empty desk. The facts are identical. What each one takes themselves to be is not. An old Indian saying is about exactly this, and the Ashtavakra Gita puts it in its first chapter.
screen: `THE SAME LAYOFF.` → `I'M FINISHED. OR: WHAT NOW?` → `WHAT EACH TAKES THEMSELVES TO BE.`

segments.voice: The verse, paraphrased: whoever takes themselves to be free is free, and whoever takes themselves to be bound is bound. And it adds: the popular saying is true, as you think, so you become. Ya matih sa gatih. Where the mind goes, there you go. This isn't positive thinking, or talking yourself into a good mood. It's about identity. Take yourself to be the body, the job, the moods, and you'll feel bound by all of them. Know yourself as the witness, and the chains were never locked. That's the end of our jnana week. Neti neti, not this, not this. The tenth man who forgot to count himself. Maitreyi, who turned down the fortune, and Shankara's hearing, reflecting, soaking in. The lane in Kashi. The boy with eight bends. And today: as you think, so you become. It's also the end of three weeks on the three paths. Karma: offer the work. Bhakti: love as the road. Jnana: who am I? Some teachers present them as separate roads suited to different temperaments, the doer, the lover, the thinker. Vivekananda did, and added a fourth, raja yoga, the path of meditation. Others say they braid together, and point to the Gita, which weaves all three through its chapters. Hindus disagree, happily, about which road to lean on. Nobody here is asking you to choose; you've walked a stretch of each. Next, the path goes deeper into two great schools, starting with the one that says: not two.
screen: `FREE IF YOU TAKE YOURSELF AS FREE.` · `AS YOU THINK, SO YOU BECOME.` · `THE DOER, THE LOVER, THE KNOWER.` · `THREE ROADS, OFTEN BRAIDED.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Try the three paths in one sitting: for karma, think of one piece of work waiting for you, and offer it; for bhakti, bring to mind someone or something you love, and let that love be there. Then, for jnana, ask quietly who is offering, who is loving, and don't answer; just rest as the one who's asking. If a sense of freedom comes, let it; if it doesn't, that's fine too.
Jnana yoga, the path of knowledge: knowing yourself as the witness. Today's verse: whoever takes themselves as free is free. As you think, so you become.
Your line: who am I? Bound or free, the verse says, begins with what you take yourself to be. And that's the three paths, walked.
